newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Britain may extend Eurotunnel licence.
newsitem.headline: France, Britain may extend Eurotunnel licence.

text.p: The French finance ministry said on Tuesday the French and British governments were ready conditionally to extend Eurotunnel's licence to run the Channel Tunnel to at least 99 years from the present 65 years.

Anglo-French firm Eurotunnel SA/plc badly needs that extension, to woo dissident shareholders due to vote on July 10 on a make-or-break deal to refinance 70 billion francs ($12 billion) of bank loans. The present licence runs until 2052.
Executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle has said Eurotunnel faces bankrupcty if investors throw out the debt plan.
But Paris and London attached conditions to the lifeline.

The company must secure approval from the shareholders and 174 creditor banks on the debt plan and it must pay a share of profits to the governments from 2052, when the extension kicks in, and for the rest of the duration of the licence, the finance ministry said in a statement.

Ponsolle said in a statement on Tuesday night that he was "extremely pleased for our shareholders about today's statement of the British and French governments relating to the extension of our concession".

He added: "It is quite legitimate, in my opinion, that an extension of the concession up to at least 99 years in total allows our shareholders to have a reasonable hope of a satisfactory return on their initial investment.
"I would have liked to reach a complete and definitive agreement but the statement of the two governments represents a decisive step towards such an agreement," he added.
The governments also have to agree ways of boosting rail freight traffic through the tunnel, the French finance ministry said.

Ponsolle had said that the company aimed to reach final agreement on these issues before a planned capital increase and the issue of free share warrants for shareholders. The warrants had been promised if the extension were granted.

But the French finance ministry said the governments could not stop the banks from taking over the tunnel concession if they exercised their rights under a "substitution clause" in their lending agreement.
The French minister for finance, economy and industry, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, welcomed the extension agreement, a separate statement from the minister said.
"The extension of the concession opens significant opportunities for development for this great European project," it said. "This agreement is the states' contribution to Eurotunnel's problems."
Christian Cambier, head of the Eurotunnel Shareholders Association, a group representing small investors, earlier said he would support the debt plan if the licence were extended.
"If there is no extension to the concession, I will vote 'no' he told Reuters. But If there were an extension, "I would vote yes."
Adacte, another smaller, more radical group of investors, has said it would reject the debt deal because there would still be significant financial risk even after the debt restructuring.

The news was the second big break for Eurotunnel in two days after Monday's announcement that a big U.S. investor had switched from opposing the restructuring and would vote for the refinancing deal at a July 10 meeting.

Eurotunnel said on Monday that U.S. fund Northern Cross Investments, which holds about three percent of the capital, has dropped its opposition to the refinancing and will back the management when the shareholders vote next week.

Shareholders have seen their investments plunge since the company came to the market in the late 1980s. The Tunnel opened late and over-budget due to building delays, suffered problems in servicing its debt and then a severe fire last November disrupted passenger and freight service.
